fetched_contents.text: Practice recommendations for the use of sedation in routine hospital-based colonoscopy Abstract Objective Although sedation improves patient experience during colonoscopy, there is great jurisdictional variability in sedative practices. The objective of this study was to develop practice recommendations for the use of moderate and deep sedation in routine hospital-based colonoscopy to facilitate standardisation of practice. Design We recruited 32 multidisciplinary panellists to participate in a modified Delphi process to establish consensus-based recommendations for the use of sedation in colonoscopy. Panel members participated in a values assessment survey followed by two rounds of anonymous online voting on preliminary practice recommendations. An inperson meeting was held between voting rounds to facilitate consensus-building. Consensus was defined as >60% agreement/disagreement with recommendation statements; >80% agreement/disagreement was considered indicative of strong consensus. Results Twenty-nine panellists participated in the values assessment survey. Panellists ranked all factors presented as important to the development of practice recommendations. The factor considered most important was patient safety. Patient satisfaction, procedural efficiency, and cost were considered less important. Strong consensus was achieved for all nine practice recommendations presented to the panel. These recommendations included that all endoscopists be able to perform colonoscopy with moderate sedation, that an endoscopist and a single trained nurse are sufficient for performing colonoscopy with moderate sedation, and that anaesthesia-provided deep sedation be used for select patients. Conclusion The recommendations presented in this study were agreed on by a multidisciplinary group and provide guidance for the use of sedation in routine hospital-based colonoscopy. Standardised sedation practices will promote safe, effective, and efficient colonoscopy for all patients. Keywords: endoscopy, colonoscopy, screening ---------------------------------------- Summary box. What is already known about this subject? * Sedation improves patient experience during endoscopy; however, there is wide variation in sedation practices. What are the new findings? * Using consensus-based methods, an expert panel established recommendations for the use of sedation in colonoscopy; this study provides nine recommendations for sedation practice in colonoscopy. * These include the recommendation that all endoscopists be capable of performing colonoscopy under moderate sedation, with the assistance of a single trained nurse; and that select patients, such as those with severe comorbidities, may benefit from the presence of an anaesthesia provider during colonoscopy, irrespective of the level of sedation. * Further to this, the panel identified specific patient groups and contexts that should warrant consideration for deep sedation, including patients who are chronic opiate users, those who have previously not tolerated endoscopy under moderate sedation, and when a lengthy or complex procedure is anticipated. How might it impact on clinical practice in the foreseeable future? * This study provides consensus-based recommendations to guide the use of sedation in colonoscopy. * These recommendations can be used to facilitate standardisation of sedation practices for routine, in-hospital colonoscopy, ensuring high-quality colonoscopy for all patients. Introduction Colonoscopy is an essential tool for the diagnosis and treatment of many intestinal conditions, including colorectal cancer. Patient pain and discomfort experienced during colonoscopy can necessitate early termination of the procedure prior to complete colonic visualisation and can lead to reluctance to undergo future procedures.1 Patient anxiety prior to and during the procedure may also be considerable and limit willingness to undergo colonoscopy. Therefore, strategies to optimise patient experience are important. Sedation provides analgesia and anxiolysis during endoscopy and is recommended for most patients undergoing colonoscopy.2 Moderate sedation, commonly provided by a combination of midazolam and fentanyl, is usually administered by an endoscopist and monitored by a nurse, with no additional healthcare providers required. Patients sedated to this level are rousable with minimal tactile stimulation.3 In contrast, deep sedation with propofol can potentially alter cardiorespiratory function and even progress to general anaesthesia. Given this risk, in Ontario, propofol is delivered by individuals qualified to administer general anaesthesia—most commonly a trained anaesthesia professional who is responsible only for monitoring the patient3–6—even if moderate sedation with propofol is intended. Deeply sedated patients require repeated or painful stimulation to be roused.3 Deep sedation can be appealing for endoscopy as propofol has a quick onset and short plasma half-life,7 which can potentially enhance procedural efficiency,8 and is believed to result in greater patient satisfaction than moderate sedation.9 10 There are wide variations in sedation practices globally and regionally.11 In the UK, approximately 10% of colonoscopies are performed without sedation, <1% are performed with propofol, and the remainder are performed with moderate sedation.12 In contrast, in 2009, 12% of Canadian endoscopists reported use of propofol,13 and importantly 50% of gastroenterologists who were not using propofol expressed interest in its routine use,13 portending a rise in its popularity. In Ontario, Canada, the use of propofol has been quickly increasing. Introduction The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) broadly considers anesthesia services as including moderate and deep sedation. Sedation is routinely used during gastrointestinal endoscopic procedures and can be defined as a drug-induced depression in the level of consciousness. The level of sedation during gastrointestinal endoscopy should be titrated to achieve a safe, comfortable and technically successful endoscopic procedure. Levels of sedation range from minimal to moderate, and from deep to general anesthesia. When endoscopic procedures are performed under moderate sedation, during moderate sedation, patients maintain their airways and are easily arousable to verbal or tactile stimulation. During deep sedation, a patient may still respond purposefully to repeated or painful stimulation but airway support may be required. During general anesthesia, patients are unarousable even with painful stimuli and often airway management is required. Sedation is a continuum. Since it is not always possible to predict how an individual patient will respond, providers administering minimal or moderate sedation should be able to support patients who enter a state of deep sedation (and those administering deep sedation should be able to support patients who enter a state of general anesthesia). Patients must be appropriately evaluated both prior to and after receiving sedation.1 In general, standards address the qualifications of those administering sedation and anesthesia and the pre- and post-anesthesia assessment. Best practices for informed consent and pre-procedure preparation

For colonoscopy with moderate sedation, informed consent should include a discussion of benefits, risks, and alternatives. The evidence indicates that informed consent is a requirement for interventional GI procedures and that its standardization remains a challenge, so the conversation should be clear and tailored to the patient’s understanding [N2-R3]. The ASGE source emphasizes that informed consent should involve a discussion of benefits, risks, and alternatives, and that patients should be appropriately evaluated before and after receiving sedation [N5-R2]. In the context of colonoscopy, the consent process should also explain what moderate sedation entails: a minimally decreased level of consciousness that allows the patient to retain the ability to breathe independently [N2-R2]. The BSG 2023 guidelines reinforce that patients should receive comprehensive information about what to expect from endoscopy and that they should be involved in shared decision-making when choosing sedation, including the option for no sedation and alternatives [N3-F3].

Patients should receive information on:
- the procedure itself and what sedation will do,
- the expected level of consciousness,
- the need to remain arousable and able to breathe,
- possible risks and complications,
- alternatives to sedation, including no sedation or other agents,
- the need for follow-up and recovery instructions [N2-R2][N3-F3][N5-R2].

Documentation of informed consent should be thorough but not merely signed. The BSG guidelines specifically recommend that patients receive comprehensive information and that shared decision-making be used where possible, with a strong emphasis on the patient’s understanding [N3-F3]. The ASGE source also notes that informed consent should be documented and that patients must be evaluated before and after sedation [N5-R2]. In practice, this means the consent form should reflect the discussion, include the patient’s understanding, and be signed after the patient has had a chance to ask questions and confirm that the information has been explained [N2-R3][N5-R2].

For outpatient or non-urgent procedures, the evidence suggests that the timing of consent matters. One source notes that it has become common practice to obtain informed consent on the day of the procedure, but it also suggests that the time and setting should be considered carefully [N5-R5]. This supports a practical workflow in which consent is obtained before the procedure and repeated or clarified if the patient’s understanding is uncertain. The BSG guidelines also recommend that patients be involved in shared decision-making where possible and that the type and amount of sedation be tailored to patient factors and the procedure itself [N3-F3]. In outpatient settings, this means the consent process should be structured so the patient has time to absorb the information and ask questions before deciding to proceed.

Special considerations include the need to document patient understanding, avoid rushed or perfunctory consent, and adjust the process if the patient has special needs or language barriers. The evidence does not provide a single standardized template, but it does support a model in which consent is part of a pre-procedure risk-balance conversation and documented as part of the sedation record [N2-R3][N5-R2][N3-F3].

Risk-based workflow and consent documentation workflow

Before sedation, patient risk should be assessed by balancing patient factors, procedure type, duration, complexity, and physical status against the intended aim of the procedure. The BSG 2023 guidelines explicitly recommend pre-assessment to tailor doses dependent on patient factors, procedure type and duration, complexity, and the physical status of the patient [N3-F3]. They also recommend enhanced periprocedural monitoring for patients with obstructive sleep apnoea (OSA) or a high BMI, because these patients may be at increased risk of periprocedural apnoea [N3-F3]. This supports a risk-based workflow that includes:
- patient history and comorbidities,
- procedure complexity and expected duration,
- pre-existing sleep-related breathing disorders,
- medication use,
- any recent procedures or interventions,
- baseline cardiopulmonary and neurological status [N3-F3].

The documentation needed for consent and sedation record should be comprehensive enough to support the decision and the safety of the procedure. The ASGE source notes that patients must be appropriately evaluated before and after receiving sedation [N5-R2], and that the CMS conditions for coverage require pre- and post-anesthesia evaluation [N1-F2]. In practice, this means the record should include:
- the patient’s name, date of birth, and procedure date,
- the patient’s indication for sedation,
- the level of sedation planned,
- the agents and dosages selected,
- the reason for selecting those agents,
- any pre-procedure risk factors,
- the patient’s understanding and consent,
- monitoring parameters recorded before, during, and after the procedure,
- any complications observed,
- recovery status and discharge instructions [N5-R2][N1-F2][N3-F3].

The evidence also suggests that documentation should be tied to the actual sedation level. The ASGE source states that moderate sedation is defined as a drug-induced depression in the level of consciousness, with patients maintaining airways and being easily arousable to verbal or tactile stimulation, while deep sedation may require repeated or painful stimulation to arouse the patient [N1-F2]. The BSG guidelines similarly emphasize that the type and amount of sedation should be tailored and that patient comfort and sedation should be continually assessed and recorded [N3-F3]. This means documentation should distinguish moderate from deep sedation, include monitoring parameters, and capture any deviations from planned care.

Handling exceptions or special circumstances should be built into the workflow. The BSG guidelines recommend that patients with OSA or high BMI receive enhanced monitoring [N3-F3]. They also recommend that anaesthetic team involvement is required when deeper sedation or general anaesthesia is used [N3-F3]. In practice, exceptions may include:
- patients with sleep apnoea,
- patients on long-term opioid therapy,
- patients with significant comorbidities,
- patients who have not tolerated previous sedation,
- patients with expected lengthy or complex procedures,
- patients with language barriers or cognitive limitations [N1-F1][N3-F3].

In such cases, the workflow should include:
- additional pre-procedure assessment,
- involvement of anaesthesia services if appropriate,
- enhanced monitoring during the procedure,
- documentation of the reason for the exception,
- updated consent if the planned level of sedation changes,
- post-procedure evaluation of recovery and complications [N1-F1][N3-F3][N5-R2].

Official guidelines and recommendations for moderate sedation in colonoscopy

The official bodies and guidelines specifically addressing routine colonoscopy sedation are the British Society of Gastroenterology (BSG) 2023 guidelines on sedation in gastrointestinal endoscopy and the ASGE policy and procedure reference guide on sedation and anesthesia [N1-F2][N3-F3]. The BSG guidelines are explicitly focused on sedation for gastrointestinal endoscopy and provide a detailed update incorporating recent advances [N3-F3]. The ASGE source is an official endoscopy society guideline set that includes a dedicated reference guide for ambulatory surgical centers and CMS Conditions for Coverage related to sedation and anesthesia [N1-F2]. The N1 evidence also includes a consensus-based practice recommendation for routine hospital-based colonoscopy, which was developed through a modified Delphi process and represents an official expert consensus statement [N1-F1].

For average-risk patients, the evidence supports a conservative approach. The consensus recommendations for routine hospital-based colonoscopy state that all endoscopists should be able to perform colonoscopy with moderate sedation, that an endoscopist and a single trained nurse are sufficient for moderate sedation, and that anaesthesia-provided deep sedation should be used for select patients rather than routinely [N1-F1]. The BSG guidelines similarly recommend alternatives to sedation, including no sedation, inhalational agents, and other adjuncts, and emphasize shared decision-making around sedation choice [N3-F3]. They also state that sedation should be tailored to patient factors, procedure type, duration, complexity, and physical status, with a strong recommendation to involve patients in decision-making where possible [N3-F3]. This suggests that for average-risk patients, moderate sedation should be the default when sedation is used, not the strongest sedation level, and that the decision should be individualized.

The recommended sedation agents and dosing ranges for average-risk patients are not fully standardized across the evidence, but the consensus recommendations do provide a practical framework. The consensus report states that moderate sedation is commonly provided by a combination of midazolam and fentanyl, and that propofol can be used for deep sedation with anaesthesia assistance [N1-F1]. The BSG guidelines recommend alternatives to sedation, including no sedation, inhalational agents, and other adjuncts, and they explicitly state that deeper sedation using propofol or general anaesthesia requires anaesthetic team involvement [N3-F3]. The N6 evidence adds dosing context: typical regimens for sedation include midazolam with opioid adjuncts, and the evidence also notes that propofol and dexmedetomidine are emerging agents being studied in colonoscopy [N6-R1][N6-R2]. However, the evidence does not provide a single uniform average-risk dosing range for all agents; instead, it supports titration to the desired level of sedation and dose adjustment based on patient factors and procedure complexity [N3-F3][N1-F1].

Monitoring requirements and safety thresholds for moderate sedation are clearly emphasized. The ASGE source defines moderate sedation as a drug-induced depression in the level of consciousness in which patients maintain airways and are easily arousable to verbal or tactile stimulation [N1-F2]. It also states that providers administering minimal or moderate sedation should be able to support patients who enter deep sedation, and that patients must be appropriately evaluated before and after receiving sedation [N1-F2]. The BSG guidelines recommend pre-assessment, monitoring of pulse, blood pressure, oxygen saturations, and respiratory rates before and after the procedure, and they recommend supplemental oxygen where any level of sedation is used [N3-F3]. The evidence also highlights that patients should not drive, operate machinery, sign legal documents, or make important decisions for 24 hours after sedation [N3-F3]. These monitoring requirements and safety thresholds support a workflow in which continuous observation is expected during sedation, and recovery is documented alongside the procedure record.

In summary, the official guidelines point to a risk-tailored approach: moderate sedation is appropriate for routine colonoscopy, especially when performed by an endoscopist with a trained nurse, and deeper sedation should be used only for select patients [N1-F1][N3-F3]. The evidence supports midazolam-fentanyl combinations, propofol in anaesthesia-assisted settings, and alternatives including no sedation or inhalational agents [N1-F1][N3-F3]. Monitoring should include airway maintenance, arousal testing, and continuous post-procedure evaluation, with additional precautions for patients at higher risk [N1-F2][N3-F3].

The evidence base for colonoscopy sedation includes midazolam, opioids, propofol, and newer agents such as dexmedetomidine, with some study-level support for ketamine and other adjuncts. The BSG 2023 guidelines specifically recommend alternatives to sedation, including no sedation, inhalational agents, and other adjuncts, and they emphasize shared decision-making when choosing sedation [N3-F3]. They also note that deeper sedation using propofol or general anaesthesia requires anaesthetic team involvement [N3-F3]. The N3 evidence further states that the most common agents for endoscopic sedation are benzodiazepines (midazolam), opioids, and propofol, and that procedural sedation and analgesia is crucial for improving patient comfort and procedural success [N3-R2][N3-R3]. The N6 evidence adds that propofol, midazolam, and dexmedetomidine are used in colonoscopy, with some study-level comparisons of these agents [N6-R1][N6-R3].

Midazolam is the most commonly referenced agent in the evidence. The consensus report states that moderate sedation is commonly provided by a combination of midazolam and fentanyl [N1-F1]. The BSG guidelines recommend benzodiazepines with or without opiates and note that shared decision-making should be used for sedation choice [N3-F3]. The evidence for dosing is mixed but consistent with titration. One source mentions a typical dosing regimen of 0.02–0.1 mg/kg IV as a bolus with additional increments as needed [N6-R1], while another source gives a usual total dose of 2.5 to 5 mg for midazolam with a maximal dosage of 6 to 7.5 mg for routine endoscopic procedures [N6-R2]. This suggests that midazolam is usually used in combination with an opioid, and that the dose is adjusted to the desired level of sedation rather than a single fixed range.

Propofol is evidence-supported but is described more as an option for deeper sedation rather than routine average-risk sedation. The consensus report says that propofol can be used for deep sedation with anaesthesia assistance [N1-F1], and the BSG guidelines state that deeper sedation using propofol or general anaesthesia requires anaesthetic team involvement [N3-F3]. The evidence also notes that propofol can alter cardiorespiratory function and may progress to general anaesthesia, which is why some systems require anaesthesia professionals to administer it [N1-F1]. The dosing in the evidence is not given as a single standard range, but the N6 evidence indicates that propofol is used in sedation regimens and that dosing is titrated to the desired level of sedation [N6-R1]. This supports a preference for propofol in anaesthesia-assisted settings rather than routine average-risk sedation.

Dexmedetomidine is the newer agent with emerging evidence. The N6 evidence shows that a study used dexmedetomidine 0.3 µg/kg bolus followed by titrated doses during colonoscopy [N6-R3]. Another N6 source notes that a study compared dexmedetomidine, ketamine, and midazolam in combination with propofol among cancer patients undergoing GI endoscopy [N6-R4]. This indicates that dexmedetomidine is being studied as an alternative agent, but the evidence provided is limited to study-level mentions rather than a broad consensus recommendation. The Medscape excerpt also notes that guidelines recommend either propofol or dexmedetomidine over benzodiazepines for sedation in critically ill, mechanically ventilated patients, though that context is not identical to routine colonoscopy [N3-R4]. Still, it suggests that dexmedetomidine may be considered as a newer option when benzodiazepines are less desirable.

Relative risks and administration requirements vary by agent. Midazolam is widely used but carries the risk of respiratory depression, especially when combined with other sedatives, and may require titration to avoid oversedation [N3-R2][N3-R3]. Propofol has a quicker onset and shorter plasma half-life, which may improve procedural efficiency, but it also carries a higher risk of cardiorespiratory depression and may require anaesthesia assistance [N1-F1]. Dexmedetomidine is an alpha-2 agonist with sedative and analgesic effects; its evidence here is mainly study-level, but it is presented as a possible alternative in the BSG guidelines and in the N6 evidence [N3-F3][N6-R3]. The evidence does not clearly establish a single preferred agent for average-risk colonoscopy; rather, it supports a choice based on patient factors, procedure complexity, and the need to avoid oversedation [N1-F1][N3-F3].

In average-risk patients, the evidence suggests that midazolam-fentanyl combinations are commonly used and preferred for routine moderate sedation [N1-F1][N3-F3]. Propofol is preferred when deeper sedation is intended and anaesthesia assistance is available [N1-F1][N3-F3]. Dexmedetomidine is supported as an emerging alternative, but the evidence provided is less robust and more study-based than for midazolam and propofol [N6-R3][N6-R4]. Overall, the evidence does not strongly recommend one agent over another for average-risk colonoscopy; instead, it supports a flexible, patient-tailored approach with careful monitoring and dose titration [N3-F3][N1-F1].

One source notes that it has become common practice to obtain informed consent on the day of the procedure, but it also suggests that the time and setting should be considered carefully [N5-R5]. This supports a practical workflow in which consent is obtained before the procedure and repeated or clarified if the patient’s understanding is uncertain. The BSG guidelines also recommend that patients be involved in shared decision-making where possible and that the type and amount of sedation be tailored to patient factors and the procedure itself [N3-F3]. In outpatient settings, this means the consent process should be structured so the patient has time to absorb the information and ask questions before deciding to proceed.

## 3) Agent-specific details for new or alternative sedation meds

The evidence base for colonoscopy sedation includes midazolam, opioids, propofol, and newer agents such as dexmedetomidine, with some study-level support for ketamine and other adjuncts [N3-R2][N3-R3][N6-R1][N6-R3]. The BSG 2023 guidelines specifically recommend alternatives to sedation, including no sedation, inhalational agents, and other adjuncts, and they emphasize shared decision-making when choosing sedation [N3-F3]. They also note that deeper sedation using propofol or general anaesthesia requires anaesthetic team involvement [N3-F3].

### Evidence supporting each new agent for colonoscopy

- **Midazolam**: The consensus report states that moderate sedation is commonly provided by a combination of midazolam and fentanyl [N1-F1]. The BSG guidelines recommend benzodiazepines with or without opiates and note that shared decision-making should be used for sedation choice [N3-F3]. This is the most well-supported agent in the evidence provided.

- **Propofol**: The consensus report says that propofol can be used for deep sedation with anaesthesia assistance [N1-F1]. The BSG guidelines state that deeper sedation using propofol or general anaesthesia requires anaesthetic team involvement [N3-F3]. The evidence also notes that propofol can alter cardiorespiratory function and may progress to general anaesthesia, which is why some systems require anaesthesia professionals to administer it [N1-F1]. Propofol is supported as an option for deeper sedation, but not as a routine average-risk agent.

- **Dexmedetomidine**: The N6 evidence shows that a study used dexmedetomidine 0.3 µg/kg bolus followed by titrated doses during colonoscopy [N6-R3]. Another N6 source notes that a study compared dexmedetomidine, ketamine, and midazolam in combination with propofol among cancer patients undergoing GI endoscopy [N6-R4]. This indicates that dexmedetomidine is being studied as an alternative agent, but the evidence provided is mainly study-level and less robust than for midazolam and propofol [N6-R3][N6-R4]. The Medscape excerpt also notes that guidelines recommend either propofol or dexmedetomidine over benzodiazepines for sedation in critically ill, mechanically ventilated patients, though that context is not identical to routine colonoscopy [N3-R4].

### Relative risks, dosing, and administration requirements

- **Midazolam**: Midazolam is widely used and typically combined with an opioid. The evidence supports titration rather than a single fixed dose, with one source mentioning a typical dosing regimen of 0.02–0.1 mg/kg IV as a bolus with additional increments as needed [N6-R1]. Another source gives a usual total dose of 2.5 to 5 mg for midazolam, with a maximal dosage of 6 to 7.5 mg for routine endoscopic procedures [N6-R2]. This supports a preference for midazolam-fentanyl combinations in routine moderate sedation.

- **Propofol**: Propofol is evidence-supported for deeper sedation but is described more as an option requiring anaesthesia assistance. It has a quicker onset and shorter plasma half-life, which may improve procedural efficiency, but it also carries a higher risk of cardiorespiratory depression and may require anaesthesia assistance [N1-F1]. The evidence does not provide a single standard average-risk dosing range, but it supports titration to the desired level of sedation [N6-R1].

- **Dexmedetomidine**: Dexmedetomidine is an alpha-2 agonist with sedative and analgesic effects. The evidence here is mainly study-level, and it is presented as a possible alternative in the BSG guidelines and in the N6 evidence [N3-F3][N6-R3]. The evidence does not clearly establish a single preferred agent for average-risk colonoscopy; rather, it supports a flexible, patient-tailed approach with careful monitoring and dose titration [N3-F3][N1-F1].

### When each agent is preferred or avoided in average-risk patients

- **Midazolam-fentanyl combinations**: These are commonly used and preferred for routine moderate sedation [N1-F1][N3-F3].

- **Propofol**: Preferred when deeper sedation is intended and anaesthesia assistance is available [N1-F1][N3-F3].

- **Dexmedetomidine**: Supported as an emerging alternative, but the evidence provided is less robust and more study-based than for midazolam and propofol [N6-R3][N6-R4]. It may be considered in specific cases where benzodiazepines are less desirable, but the evidence here does not strongly recommend it as a routine average-risk agent.

## 4) Risk-based workflow and consent documentation workflow

Before sedation, patient risk should be assessed by balancing **patient factors, procedure type, duration, complexity, and physical status** against the intended aim of the procedure [N3-F3]. The BSG guidelines also recommend enhanced periprocedural monitoring for patients with obstructive sleep apnoea (OSA) or a high BMI, because these patients may be at increased risk of periprocedural apnoea [N3-F3]. This supports a risk-based workflow that includes:
- patient history and comorbidities,
- procedure complexity and expected duration,
- pre-existing sleep-related breathing disorders,
- medication use,
- any recent procedures or interventions,
- baseline cardiopulmonary and neurological status [N3-F3].

### What documentation is needed for consent and sedation record

The documentation needed should be comprehensive enough to support the decision and the safety of the procedure. The ASGE source notes that patients must be appropriately evaluated before and after receiving sedation [N5-R2]. The CMS conditions for coverage also require pre- and post-anesthesia evaluation [N1-F2]. In practice, this means the record should include:
- the patient’s name, date of birth, and procedure date,
- the patient’s indication for sedation,
- the level of sedation planned,
- the agents and dosages selected,
- the reason for selecting those agents,
- any pre-procedure risk factors,
- the patient’s understanding and consent,
- monitoring parameters recorded before, during, and after the procedure,
- any complications observed,
- recovery status and discharge instructions [N5-R2][N1-F2][N3-F3].

### How to handle exceptions or special circumstances in practice

The evidence also suggests that exceptions should be handled through additional pre-procedure assessment, involvement of anaesthesia services if appropriate, enhanced monitoring during the procedure, and updated documentation if the planned level of sedation changes [N1-F1][N3-F3]. In practice, exceptions may include:
- patients with sleep apnoea,
- patients on long-term opioid therapy,
- patients with significant comorbidities,
- patients who have not tolerated previous sedation,
- patients with expected lengthy or complex procedures,
- patients with language barriers or cognitive limitations [N1-F1][N3-F3].

In such cases, the workflow should include:
- additional pre-procedure assessment,
- involvement of anaesthesia services if appropriate,
- enhanced monitoring during the procedure,
- documentation of the reason for the exception,
- updated consent if the planned level of sedation changes,
- post-procedure evaluation of recovery and complications [N1-F1][N3-F3][N5-R2].

## 5) Practical conclusion for updating clinic protocols

For your clinic’s updated protocols, the strongest evidence supports a **moderate sedation-first approach** for average-risk patients, with a preference for midazolam-fentanyl combinations and a clear distinction between moderate and deeper sedation [N1-F1][N3-F3]. Dexmedetomidine is an emerging alternative with some study support, but it is not yet established as the routine choice for average-risk colonoscopy [N6-R3][N6-R4].

The BSG guidelines also recommend shared decision-making and that patients be involved in choosing the sedative medication if possible [N3-F3].

## 6) References you can reference

If you want to reference official guidelines and recommendations, the most authoritative sources are:

- **dexmedetomidine as an emerging alternative** [N6-R3][N6-R4]

- shared decision-making [N3-F3]
- documentation of patient understanding [N5-R2]
- careful timing of consent in outpatient settings [N5-R5]

## 7) Bottom line

If you are updating your clinic protocols, the evidence points to a clear framework:
- **Use moderate sedation as the default for average-risk patients**, especially midazolam-fentanyl combinations.
- **Avoid deeper sedation routinely** unless anaesthesia assistance is available and the patient’s risk profile warrants it [N1-F1][N3-F3].
- **Use dexmedetomidine selectively** as a newer alternative, but only where the evidence supports its use and the patient’s factors justify it [N6-R3][N6-R4].
- **Obtain informed consent thoroughly**, with a documented discussion of benefits, risks, alternatives, and recovery instructions [N2-R3][N5-R2][N3-F3].
- **Document the sedation record comprehensively**, including pre-procedure assessment, monitoring, dosing rationale, and recovery status [N5-R2][N1-F2][N3-F3].
- **Adjust the workflow for special circumstances**, such as OSA, high BMI, opioid use, or other comorbidities [N3-F3].

This integrated approach should help you update your clinic guidelines in a way that is evidence-based, patient-centered, and compliant with official recommendations [N1-F1][N1-F2][N3-F3].

### How to document informed consent and patient understanding

Documentation should be thorough but not merely signed. The BSG guidelines specifically recommend that patients receive comprehensive information and that shared decision-making be used where possible, with a strong emphasis on the patient’s understanding [N3-F3]. The ASGE source also notes that informed consent should be documented and that patients must be evaluated before and after receiving sedation [N5-R2]. In practice, this means the consent form should reflect the discussion, include the patient’s understanding, and be signed after the patient has had a chance to ask questions and confirm that the information has been explained [N2-R3][N5-R2].

### Special considerations for outpatient or non-urgent procedures

The evidence suggests that the timing of consent matters. One source notes that it has become common practice to obtain informed consent on the day of the procedure, but it also suggests that the time and setting should be considered carefully [N5-R5]. This supports a practical workflow in which consent is obtained before the procedure and repeated or clarified if the patient’s understanding is uncertain. The BSG guidelines also recommend that patients be involved in shared decision-making where possible and that the type and amount of sedation be tailored to patient factors and the procedure itself [N3-F3]. In outpatient settings, this means the consent process should be structured so the patient has time to absorb the information and ask questions before deciding to proceed.

## 3) Agent-specific details for new or alternative sedation meds

The evidence base for colonoscopy sedation includes midazolam, opioids, propofol, and newer agents such as dexmedetomidine, with some study-level support for ketamine and other adjuncts [N3-R2][N3-R3][N6-R1][N6-R3]. The BSG 2023 guidelines specifically recommend alternatives to sedation, including no sedation, inhalational agents, and other adjuncts, and they emphasize shared decision-making when choosing sedation [N3-F3]. They also note that deeper sedation using propofol or general anaesthesia requires anaesthetic team involvement [N3-F3].

### Evidence supporting each new agent for colonoscopy

- **Midazolam**: The consensus report states that moderate sedation is commonly provided by a combination of midazolam and fentanyl [N1-F1]. The BSG guidelines recommend benzodiazepines with or without opiates and note that shared decision-making should be used for sedation choice [N3-F3]. This is the most well-supported agent in the evidence provided.

- **Propofol**: The consensus report says that propofol can be used for deep sedation with anaesthesia assistance [N1-F1]. The BSG guidelines state that deeper sedation using propofol or general anaesthesia requires anaesthetic team involvement [N3-F3]. The evidence also notes that propofol can alter cardiorespiratory function and may progress to general anaesthesia, which is why some systems require anaesthesia professionals to administer it [N1-F1]. Propofol is supported as an option for deeper sedation, but not as a routine average-risk agent.

- **Dexmedetomidine**: The N6 evidence shows that a study used dexmedetomidine 0.3 µg/kg bolus followed by titrated doses during colonoscopy [N6-R3]. Another N6 source notes that a study compared dexmedetomidine, ketamine, and midazolam in combination with propofol among cancer patients undergoing GI endoscopy [N6-R4]. This indicates that dexmedetomidine is being studied as an alternative agent, but the evidence provided is mainly study-level and less robust than for midazolam and propofol [N6-R3][N6-R4]. The Medscape excerpt also notes that guidelines recommend either propofol or dexmedetomidine over benzodiazepines for sedation in critically ill, mechanically ventilated patients, though that context is not identical to routine colonoscopy [N3-R4].

### Relative risks, dosing, and administration requirements

- **Midazolam**: Midazolam is widely used and typically combined with an opioid. The evidence supports titration rather than a single fixed dose, with one source mentioning a typical dosing regimen of 0.02–0.1 mg/kg IV as a bolus with additional increments as needed [N6-R1]. Another source gives a usual total dose of 2.5 to 5 mg for midazolam, with a maximal dosage of 6 to 7.5 mg for routine endoscopic procedures [N6-R2]. This supports a preference for midazolam-fentanyl combinations in routine moderate sedation.

- **Propofol**: Propofol is evidence-supported for deeper sedation but is described more as an option requiring anaesthesia assistance. It has a quicker onset and shorter plasma half-life, which may improve procedural efficiency, but it also carries a higher risk of cardiorespiratory depression and may require anaesthesia assistance [N1-F1]. The evidence does not provide a single standard average-risk dosing range, but it supports titration to the desired level of sedation [N6-R1].

- **Dexmedetomidine**: Dexmedetomidine is an alpha-2 agonist with sedative and analgesic effects. The evidence here is mainly study-level, and it is presented as a possible alternative in the BSG guidelines and in the N6 evidence [N3-F3][N6-R3]. The evidence does not clearly establish a single preferred agent for average-risk colonoscopy; rather, it supports a flexible, patient-tailed approach with careful monitoring and dose titration [N3-F3][N1-F1].

### When each agent is preferred or avoided in average-risk patients

- **Midazolam-fentanyl combinations**: These are commonly used and preferred for routine moderate sedation [N1-F1][N3-F3].

- **Propofol**: Preferred when deeper sedation is intended and anaesthesia assistance is available [N1-F1][N3-F3].

- **Dexmedetomidine**: Supported as an emerging alternative, but the evidence provided is less robust and more study-based than for midazolam and propofol [N6-R3][N6-R4]. It may be considered in specific cases where benzodiazepines are less desirable, but the evidence here does not strongly recommend it as a routine average-risk agent.

## 4) Risk-based workflow and consent documentation workflow

Before sedation, patient risk should be assessed by balancing **patient factors, procedure type, duration, complexity, and physical status** against the intended aim of the procedure [N3-F3]. The BSG guidelines also recommend enhanced periprocedural monitoring for patients with obstructive sleep apnoea (OSA) or a high BMI, because these patients may be at increased risk of periprocedural apnoea [N3-F3]. This supports a risk-based workflow that includes:
- patient history and comorbidities,
- procedure complexity and expected duration,
- pre-existing sleep-related breathing disorders,
- medication use,
- any recent procedures or interventions,
- baseline cardiopulmonary and neurological status [N3-F3].

### What documentation is needed for consent and sedation record

The documentation needed should be comprehensive enough to support the decision and the safety of the procedure. The ASGE source notes that patients must be appropriately evaluated before and after receiving sedation [N5-R2]. The CMS conditions for coverage also require pre- and post-anesthesia evaluation [N1-F2]. In practice, this means the record should include:
- the patient’s name, date of birth, and procedure date,
- the patient’s indication for sedation,
- the level of sedation planned,
- the agents and dosages selected,
- the reason for selecting those agents,
- any pre-procedure risk factors,
- the patient’s understanding and consent,
- monitoring parameters recorded before, during, and after the procedure,
- any complications observed,
- recovery status and discharge instructions [N5-R2][N1-F2][N3-F3].

### How to handle exceptions or special circumstances in practice

The evidence also suggests that exceptions should be handled through additional pre-procedure assessment, involvement of anaesthesia services if appropriate, enhanced monitoring during the procedure, and updated documentation if the planned level of sedation changes [N1-F1][N3-F3]. In practice, exceptions may include:
- patients with sleep apnoea,
- patients on long-term opioid therapy,
- patients with significant comorbidities,
- patients who have not tolerated previous sedation,
- patients with expected lengthy or complex procedures,
- patients with language barriers or cognitive limitations [N1-F1][N3-F3].

In such cases, the workflow should include:
- additional pre-procedure assessment,
- involvement of anaesthesia services if appropriate,
- enhanced monitoring during the procedure,
- documentation of the reason for the exception,
- updated consent if the planned level of sedation changes,
- post-procedure evaluation of recovery and complications [N1-F1][N3-F3][N5-R2].

## 5) Practical conclusion for updating clinic protocols

For your clinic’s updated protocols, the strongest evidence supports a **moderate sedation-first approach** for average-risk patients, with a preference for midazolam-fentanyl combinations and a clear distinction between moderate and deeper sedation [N1-F1][N3-F3]. Dexmedetomidine is an emerging alternative with some study support, but it is not yet established as the routine choice for average-risk colonoscopy [N6-R3][N6-R4].

For consent, the evidence supports a **structured pre-procedure conversation** that includes benefits, risks, alternatives, and recovery instructions, with documentation tied to the patient’s understanding rather than a signed form alone [N2-R3][N5-R2][N3-F3]. The BSG guidelines also recommend shared decision-making and that patients be involved in choosing the sedative medication if possible [N3-F3].

For documentation, the evidence supports a **comprehensive sedation record** that includes patient factors, agent selection, dosing rationale, monitoring parameters, and recovery status [N5-R2][N1-F2][N3-F3].

- careful timing of consent in outpatient settings [N5-R5]

## 7) Bottom line

If you are updating your clinic protocols, the evidence points to a clear framework:
- **Use moderate sedation as the default for average-risk patients**, especially midazolam-fentanyl combinations.
- **Avoid deeper sedation routinely** unless anaesthesia assistance is available and the patient’s risk profile warrants it [N1-F1][N3-F3].
- **Use dexmedetomidine selectively** as a newer alternative, but only where the evidence supports its use and the patient’s factors justify it [N6-R3][N6-R4].
- **Obtain informed consent thoroughly**, with a documented discussion of benefits, risks, alternatives, and recovery instructions [N2-R3][N5-R2][N3-F3].
- **Document the sedation record comprehensively**, including pre-procedure assessment, monitoring, dosing rationale, and recovery status [N5-R2][N1-F2][N3-F3].
- **Adjust the workflow for special circumstances**, such as OSA, high BMI, opioid use, or other comorbidities [N3-F3].

This integrated approach should help you update your clinic guidelines in a way that is evidence-based, patient-centered, and compliant with official recommendations [N1-F1][N1-F2][N3-F3].
